solution:

So the mistake in Option D is the formation of sodium boride.

(I) Gallium has lower density than indium.

question:
Identify the correct statement from the following.

(I) Gallium has lower density than indium.

(II) Indium has a lower melting point than gallium.

(III) Ionisation energy of boron is higher than thallium.

(IV) Hydroxide of aluminium is more acidic than that of boron.

(V) The hydroxide of boron is acidic while that of aluminium is amphoteric.

Which of the following options is correct?
solution:
The correct option is A: I, III, V only.

Check each statement one by one.

(I) Gallium has lower density than indium.

This is correct.

Density of gallium is about $5.9 \ \text{g cm}^{-3}$, while density of indium is about $7.3 \ \text{g cm}^{-3}$.

So, gallium has lower density than indium.

(II) Indium has a lower melting point than gallium.

This is incorrect.

Gallium has an unusually low melting point, about $303 \ \text{K}$, while indium melts at about $430 \ \text{K}$.

So indium has a higher melting point than gallium.

(III) Ionisation energy of boron is higher than thallium.

This is correct.

In Group 13, ionisation enthalpy generally decreases down the group, although there are some irregularities due to poor shielding by $d$ and $f$ electrons.

Still, boron has higher ionisation energy than thallium.

So,

$$ IE_1(\text{B}) > IE_1(\text{Tl}) $$

(IV) Hydroxide of aluminium is more acidic than that of boron.

This is incorrect.

The hydroxide of boron, $B(OH)_3$, is acidic. Aluminium hydroxide, $Al(OH)_3$, is amphoteric.

So boron hydroxide is more acidic than aluminium hydroxide.

(V) The hydroxide of boron is acidic while that of aluminium is amphoteric.

This is correct.

$$ B(OH)_3 \text{ is acidic} $$

$$ Al(OH)_3 \text{ is amphoteric} $$

So the correct statements are:

$$ \text{I, III and V} $$

Hence, the correct answer is Option A.

question: Which of the following reactions will evolve H2 gas?
solution:
Diborane undergoes rapid hydrolysis in the presence of water to produce boric acid and hydrogen gas.

The balanced chemical equation for this reaction is:

$$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6(\text{g}) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \longrightarrow 2\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3(\text{aq}) + 6\text{H}_2(\text{g})$$

Let us quickly see what happens in the other options:

  • Reaction of $\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$ with $\text{NH}_3$ at room temperature gives an addition product (adduct), $\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 \cdot 2\text{NH}_3$, without releasing hydrogen gas immediately.

  • Reaction with $\text{O}_2$ is a combustion reaction that produces boron trioxide ($\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$) and water vapor ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$).

Thus, the reaction that readily evolves $\text{H}_2$ gas is the reaction of diborane with water.

Correct Option: Option A

question: Incorrect statement about boron trihalides is
options: All boron trihalides are covalent with low boiling points.
The order of ease of hydrolysis of trihalides of boron is $\mathrm{BF_3 < BCl_3 < BBr_3 < BI_3}$ due to strength of $p\pi$-$p\pi$ bonding.
All boron trihalides can be prepared by the treatment of halogens with a mixture of $\mathrm{B_2O_3}$ and carbon at high temperature.
Boron trifluoride can be obtained by heating $\mathrm{CaF_2}$ with concentrated sulphuric acid and boric anhydride.
solution:
Boron trihalides ($\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{BCl_3}$, $\mathrm{BBr_3}$, and $\mathrm{BI_3}$) are covalent molecules. They exist as simple monomers and have low boiling points due to weak intermolecular van der Waals forces. $\mathrm{BF_3}$ and $\mathrm{BCl_3}$ are gases, $\mathrm{BBr_3}$ is a volatile liquid, and $\mathrm{BI_3}$ is a low-melting solid. So, Statement A is correct.

In boron trihalides, the unhybridized $2p$ orbital of boron overlaps with filled $p$ orbitals of the halogen atom to form $p\pi\text{-}p\pi$ back bonding. The extent of back bonding is maximum in $\mathrm{BF_3}$ ($2p\text{-}2p$) and decreases as the size of the halogen increases:

$$\mathrm{BF_3 > BCl_3 > BBr_3 > BI_3}$$

Because of weaker back bonding, boron in $\mathrm{BI_3}$ has a stronger tendency to accept electron pairs compared to $\mathrm{BF_3}$. Consequently, the Lewis acidity and the ease of hydrolysis follow the order:

$$\mathrm{BF_3 < BCl_3 < BBr_3 < BI_3}$$

Thus, Statement B is correct.

Boron trifluoride ($\mathrm{BF_3}$) is prepared on a large scale by heating boric anhydride ($\mathrm{B_2O_3}$) with calcium fluoride and concentrated sulphuric acid:

$$\mathrm{B_2O_3 + 3CaF_2 + 3H_2SO_4 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2BF_3 + 3CaSO_4 + 3H_2O}$$

This makes Statement D correct.

The method of passing halogens over a heated mixture of $\mathrm{B_2O_3}$ and carbon works well for preparing $\mathrm{BCl_3}$ and $\mathrm{BBr_3}$:

$$\mathrm{B_2O_3 + 3C + 3Cl_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2BCl_3 + 3CO}$$

However, this method is not suitable for all trihalides. For example, $\mathrm{BF_3}$ is not prepared by this route, and $\mathrm{BI_3}$ cannot be formed effectively due to unfavourable thermodynamics. Hence, the statement that all boron trihalides can be prepared by this method is incorrect.

question:
Which of the following statements is correct?

A. Boron trioxide is acidic in nature.

B. Ammonal is a mixture of aluminium compounds and used in bombs.

C. $\mathrm{BF_3}$ exist as dimer.

D. $\mathrm{BCl_3}$ does not conduct electricity in its molten state.

E. $\mathrm{B_2O_3}$ is sesquioxide.
solution:
Correct Option: C

Statement A is correct: Boron trioxide \left(B_2 O_3\right)$ is acidic in nature. It reacts with basic (metallic) oxides to form metal borates.

Statement B is correct: Ammonal is a well-known explosive mixture consisting of aluminium powder and ammonium nitrate, commonly used in bombs.

Statement C is incorrect: $B F_3$ exists as a monomer, not a dimer. The electron deficiency of the central boron atom in the monomer is compensated by strong $p \pi-p \pi$ back bonding from the fluorine atoms, which stabilizes the molecule and prevents dimerization.

Statement D is correct: $\mathrm{BCl}_3$ is a purely covalent compound. Because it lacks ions, it does not conduct electricity in its molten state.

Statement E is correct: $B_2 O_3$ is referred to as a sesquioxide. A sesquioxide is an oxide containing three atoms of oxygen for every two atoms of the other element (a 3:2 ratio).

Therefore, statements A, B, D, and E are correct.

q:
Statement I : The hydroxides of Group 13 elements become more basic down the group.

Statement II : Unlike aluminum, boron does not form a protective oxide layer.

Which of the following is correct?
question:
Statement I : The hydroxides of Group 13 elements become more basic down the group.

Statement II : Unlike aluminum, boron does not form a protective oxide layer.

Which of the following is correct?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
solution:
Statement I: The hydroxides of Group 13 elements become more basic as we move down the group. This is correct. At the top of the group, $\mathrm{B(OH)_3}$ (boric acid) is actually acidic — it's a weak acid. Next, $\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}$ is amphoteric, meaning it can act as both an acid and a base. As we go further down to $\mathrm{Ga(OH)_3}$, $\mathrm{In(OH)_3}$, and $\mathrm{Tl(OH)_3}$, the hydroxides become increasingly basic. So the trend is: acidic → amphoteric → basic, moving down the group. Statement I is correct.

Statement II: This says that unlike aluminium, boron does not form a protective oxide layer. This is actually incorrect. Boron does form a stable oxide layer of $\mathrm{B_2O_3}$ on its surface, just like aluminium forms a layer of $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$. This oxide coating protects the element underneath from further oxidation. So boron and aluminium behave similarly in this regard.

The correct answer is: Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect.

question: Boric acid heated to red hot i.e., above 370 K gives
solution:
When orthoboric acid ($\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$) is heated, it undergoes dehydration in stages depending on the temperature.

When heated gently to about $370\text{ K}$, it first loses a molecule of water to form metaboric acid ($\text{HBO}_2$):

$$\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3 \xrightarrow{370\text{ K}} \text{HBO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

On further heating to red hot temperatures, metaboric acid breaks down completely, losing more water to form boric anhydride (boron trioxide, $\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$):

$$2\text{HBO}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Red hot}} \text{B}_2\text{O}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Thus, heating boric acid to red hot gives $\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$.

Correct Option: Option C ($\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$)

question: Alumina is insoluble in water because
options: it has high lattice energy and low heat of hydration.
it has low lattice energy and high heat of hydration.
Al3+ and O2− ions are not excessively hydrated.
solution:
For any ionic compound to dissolve in water, the energy released during the hydration of its ions (hydration enthalpy) must be greater than the energy required to break its crystal lattice (lattice energy).

$$\text{Hydration Energy} > \text{Lattice Energy} \implies \text{Soluble}$$

$$\text{Lattice Energy} > \text{Hydration Energy} \implies \text{Insoluble}$$

In alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$), the aluminum ion ($\text{Al}^{3+}$) carries a $+3$ charge and the oxide ion ($\textO^{2-}$) carries a $-2$ charge. Because of these high charges and small ionic radii, the electrostatic forces holding the ions together in the crystal lattice are extremely strong.

This gives alumina an exceptionally high lattice energy. The hydration energy released when water molecules surround the ions is not enough to overcome this strong lattice energy. As a result, alumina does not dissolve in water.

Correct Option: Option B (it has high lattice energy and low heat of hydration.)

q: When borax is heated in a bunsen burner flame with CaO and a loop of platinum wire, a blue coloured bead $X$ is formed. The number of boron atom in $X$ is $\_\_\_\_$
question: When borax is heated in a bunsen burner flame with CaO and a loop of platinum wire, a blue coloured bead $X$ is formed. The number of boron atom in $X$ is $\_\_\_\_$
solution:
When borax ($\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$) is heated on a platinum wire loop, it first loses its water of crystallization and swells up. On further heating, it melts to form a clear, transparent glassy bead composed of sodium metaborate ($\text{NaBO}_2$) and boric anhydride ($\text{B}_2\text{O}_3$).

$$\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 + 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

$$\text{Na}_2\text{B}_4\text{O}_7 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\text{NaBO}_2 + \text{B}_2\text{O}_3$$

When this hot bead is touched with a metal oxide like cobalt oxide ($\text{CoO}$) and heated again in the flame, the boric anhydride reacts with the metal oxide to form a characteristic coloured metaborate bead:

$$\text{CoO} + \text{B}_2\text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{Co(BO}_2)_2$$

The blue bead formed is cobalt metaborate, $\text{Co(BO}_2)_2$.

Looking at the chemical formula $\text{Co(BO}_2)_2$, there are $2$ boron atoms present in the compound.

The number of boron atoms in $X$ is 2.

q: How many electrons are involved in the three-center two-electron bonds in diborane $\left(\mathrm{B}_2 \mathrm{H}_6\right)$ ?
question: How many electrons are involved in the three-center two-electron bonds in diborane $\left(\mathrm{B}_2 \mathrm{H}_6\right)$ ?
solution:
In diborane ($\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6$), there are a total of $12$ valence electrons ($6$ from the two boron atoms and $6$ from the six hydrogen atoms).

The structure of diborane contains two types of bonds:

  1. Terminal $\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}$ bonds: There are $4$ terminal hydrogen atoms. Each forms a regular two-center two-electron ($2c\text{-}2e$) covalent bond with a boron atom. These $4$ bonds account for:

$$4 \times 2 = 8 \text{ electrons}$$

$$\text{Total electrons involved} = 2 \times 2 = 4 \text{ electrons}$$

Therefore, $4$ electrons are involved in the three-center two-electron bonds in diborane.

question:
Determine the number of $\pi$-bonds present in a molecule of borazine \left(\mathrm{B}_3 \mathrm{~N}_3 \mathrm{H}_6\right)$, often referred to as "inorganic benzene".

$
solution:
In borazine, $\mathrm{B_3N_3H_6}$, the ring has alternate boron and nitrogen atoms:

$$ \mathrm{B-N-B-N-B-N} $$

Each boron and nitrogen atom is $sp^2$ hybridised, so the ring is planar. The unhybridised $p$ orbitals overlap sideways.

Nitrogen has a lone pair, while boron has an empty $p$ orbital. Due to this, $\pi$-bonding takes place between $\mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{N}$ atoms around the ring.

Borazine is isoelectronic with benzene, so just like benzene it has a delocalised $\pi$-system containing $6$ $\pi$-electrons. This corresponds to:

$$ 3 \pi\text{-bonds} $$

So, the number of $\pi$-bonds in borazine is:

$$ \boxed{3} $$

q: Boranes are readily hydrolysed by water to give 'compound $A^{\prime}$. The number of oxygen atom in compound ' $A$ ' is $\_\_\_\_$.
question: Boranes are readily hydrolysed by water to give 'compound $A^{\prime}$. The number of oxygen atom in compound ' $A$ ' is $\_\_\_\_$.
solution:
Boranes, such as diborane ($\text{B}_2\text{H}_6$), readily undergo hydrolysis when reacted with water.

During this reaction, the boron-hydrogen bonds break to form orthoboric acid (commonly called boric acid) along with the release of hydrogen gas.

The balanced chemical equation for the reaction is:

$$\text{B}_2\text{H}_6 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow 2\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3 + 6\text{H}_2$$

Here, compound 'A' is boric acid, which has the chemical formula $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$ (or $\text{B(OH)}_3$).

Looking at the formula $\text{H}_3\text{BO}_3$, each molecule contains:

  • 1 Boron ($\text{B}$) atom

  • 3 Hydrogen ($\text{H}$) atoms

  • 3 Oxygen ($\text{O}$) atoms

The number of oxygen atoms in compound 'A' is 3.
